The 4% take-profit is there to harvest the run-up before the print and the 6% stop to cap the coin-flip if I am still holding into it.

trades.why: Memory is the binding physical constraint of the AI buildout, and Amazon just attributed its $20bn capex raise specifically to higher memory costs - the largest buyer's cost line is Micron's revenue line. HBM is sold out through 2026 under multi-year agreements, DRAM rose 90% in Q1 with suppliers guiding a further 10-20% per month into year-end, and Micron forecasts shortage beyond 2026. +212% YTD and +637% over a year makes it the strongest trend in my mandate's named universe; largest weight, wide -18% stop because its realised volatility is extreme and a tight stop would just donate the position to noise. [Weekly desk 2026-08-01: My short sleeve was built on one explicit claim, which I wrote down: hyperscalers are trapped, because cutting capex collapses orders and keeping capex gets the stock hit like Meta's was. Amazon ran that experiment 36 hours later - raised the capex guide by $20bn to $220bn, showed AWS accelerating 28% to 37% with a $496bn backlog - and the stock rose 15.6%. Microsoft did the same on Azure and rose 16%. The demand signal the AI-capex drawdown was pricing has been falsified by the two largest buyers, and SOXX responded +8% in a session. This is not noise around my thesis, it is the specific event my thesis said could not happen, and it postdates the reasoning I recorded on 7/30. Momentum discipline means following the trend that exists, and the trend that existed for one month has just been reversed by dated fundamentals, so I cover all four shorts (SOXX, ORCL, SOXL, TSLA) rather than carry an 18% gross short into a sector-wide squeeze - ORCL especially, because a $638bn backlog at a 52-week low after a 40% retrace is the single most squeezable name in the group once cloud demand is confirmed. I also cut AAPL: I owned it as the best large-cap trend AND as the anti-capex winner, and both legs broke at once when it fell 7.3% on a weak September guide, with Cook's chip-supply squeeze being precisely the input-cost story that makes Micron money and costs Apple margin. So I express that same insight on the correct side. What I do NOT do is whipsaw the whole book: XLV, RTX, LMT, XLE and VZ were never invalidated by this news - healthcare is still the best multi-horizon trend, and the Hormuz standoff plus intercepted Iranian missiles actively reinforce defense and energy - so they stay as ballast at reduced size while the mandate's home position, leveraged long semis, comes back with real size and real stops. XLP goes because in a levered growth-momentum book staples were always the weakest claim on capital and it duplicates my Round 3 exposure. Net result is 90% gross long, ~41% of it low-beta ballast, 10% cash at 4%, and no forced short - there is no falsified trend to short right now, and crypto is still directionless, so paying costs to manufacture a hedge would be theatre. Turnover here costs roughly 2bps a side against the risk of carrying a falsified short into a confirmed reversal; the cost is not the binding consideration, being wrong is.]

trades.fee_schedule: equities/ETFs 2bps (5bps leveraged, 12bps sub-$15) + 0.31bps SEC/TAF on sells; crypto spot 35bps; perps 7.5bps notional + 10% APR funding; short borrow 3% APR
trades.why: Post-earnings breakout (+10.5% 1w, +14.9% 1m, +23.0% 3m) that has since been reinforced by live escalation - US forces intercepting an Iranian ballistic-missile attack and an unresolved Hormuz standoff. This is order-book momentum, indifferent to whether hyperscaler capex is loved or hated in any given week. [Weekly desk 2026-08-01: My short sleeve was built on one explicit claim, which I wrote down: hyperscalers are trapped, because cutting capex collapses orders and keeping capex gets the stock hit like Meta's was. Amazon ran that experiment 36 hours later - raised the capex guide by $20bn to $220bn, showed AWS accelerating 28% to 37% with a $496bn backlog - and the stock rose 15.6%. Microsoft did the same on Azure and rose 16%. The demand signal the AI-capex drawdown was pricing has been falsified by the two largest buyers, and SOXX responded +8% in a session. This is not noise around my thesis, it is the specific event my thesis said could not happen, and it postdates the reasoning I recorded on 7/30. Momentum discipline means following the trend that exists, and the trend that existed for one month has just been reversed by dated fundamentals, so I cover all four shorts (SOXX, ORCL, SOXL, TSLA) rather than carry an 18% gross short into a sector-wide squeeze - ORCL especially, because a $638bn backlog at a 52-week low after a 40% retrace is the single most squeezable name in the group once cloud demand is confirmed. I also cut AAPL: I owned it as the best large-cap trend AND as the anti-capex winner, and both legs broke at once when it fell 7.3% on a weak September guide, with Cook's chip-supply squeeze being precisely the input-cost story that makes Micron money and costs Apple margin. So I express that same insight on the correct side. What I do NOT do is whipsaw the whole book: XLV, RTX, LMT, XLE and VZ were never invalidated by this news - healthcare is still the best multi-horizon trend, and the Hormuz standoff plus intercepted Iranian missiles actively reinforce defense and energy - so they stay as ballast at reduced size while the mandate's home position, leveraged long semis, comes back with real size and real stops. XLP goes because in a levered growth-momentum book staples were always the weakest claim on capital and it duplicates my Round 3 exposure. Net result is 90% gross long, ~41% of it low-beta ballast, 10% cash at 4%, and no forced short - there is no falsified trend to short right now, and crypto is still directionless, so paying costs to manufacture a hedge would be theatre. Turnover here costs roughly 2bps a side against the risk of carrying a falsified short into a confirmed reversal; the cost is not the binding consideration, being wrong is.]

trades.fee_schedule: equities/ETFs 2bps (5bps leveraged, 12bps sub-$15) + 0.31bps SEC/TAF on sells; crypto spot 35bps; perps 7.5bps notional + 10% APR funding; short borrow 3% APR
trades.why: GE Vernova: the power-generation bottleneck, and the one input in the AI stack that cannot be conjured away by extending depreciation schedules. $720-745B of 2026 hyperscaler capex has to be fed electrons. Q2 orders +88% y/y, backlog $176B, gas-turbine capacity target raised to 30GW by 2030, Morgan Stanley target $1,350 vs $990 spot. Held flat rather than added because at PE 28.3 and within 17% of its 52-week high it is my largest and least-discounted leg. [Weekly desk 2026-08-01: I set Thursday's book on the premise that the market had switched to paying for capex DISCIPLINE, and that premise was falsified within hours of my decision by a print I could not see: Amazon raised 2026 capex to $220B from $200B, said it still cannot meet demand, and was rewarded +15%, taking the four hyperscalers to $720-745B for 2026, +77% y/y. The market paid 15% for Microsoft cutting and 15% for Amazon raising - it is paying for AI revenue, not restraint. My names were right for the wrong reason; my SIZING was wrong, because I set 20% cash and 80% gross as insurance against a spending slowdown that is not happening. So I am redeploying cash rather than rebuilding: nothing is sold, no thesis is reversed, and equity costs of 2bps make an 8-point redeployment effectively free. Crucially, Jassy named the reason for the $20B raise as MEMORY COST - the same fact Samsung confirmed by warning supply stays tight into 2028. That is one fact that pays three of my legs at once: it forces DRAM wafer-fab-equipment spend (AMAT), it makes custom silicon the cheaper compute-per-dollar answer as budgets inflate (AVGO), and it is the input-cost squeeze that destroys a ~10%-gross-margin assembler (SMCI short). I add where the confirmation is not yet in the price - AMAT 16-to-21 and AVGO 13-to-16, both still 21-31% below their highs and 24-29% below consensus targets - and deliberately do NOT add to MU, whose thesis was confirmed most loudly but which ran +18.4% then +5% straight into my fill and is +212% YTD; chasing that is how you buy a memory cyclical at the top. I hold ANET flat rather than size into a binary Aug 4 print, and hold GEV at 22% because it is already my largest leg and, at PE 28.3 and within 17% of its high, it is no longer the discount it was. I keep the 3x-semis kicker at ZERO despite the bullish capex news: with AMAT, AVGO and MU already 49% of the book, a leveraged semis ETF adds no new idea, only correlation to my largest exposure, and the rate backdrop got worse this week, not better. And I keep 12% cash rather than going to zero for exactly that reason - the 10y at 4.73% is a one-year high and the Fed gave no forward guidance with a September hike heavily priced, so I am buying the confirmed fundamental while retaining a real buffer against the multiple risk.]

Q2 beat at $7.61 adj vs $7.22 with revenue +26%, then fell 6.7% purely on unchanged guidance; the 2027 exit from plans covering ~600k members is margin-accretive toward the 3% pretax target. A derated entry into the sector printing all-time highs as capital leaves the AI trade. Upsized from 4.25%. [Unrestricted-retail resize (2026-07-30, free internet + no sizing caps): The screen that built this book is stale in exactly the way a dispersion manager must react to. Four of my twelve longs - MU, DELL, PLTR and CRM - were selected for high residual-to-SPY volatility, but that residual has since collapsed into a single common factor: the AI capex trade. SOX -19% MTD (worst month since 2008), $1trn of chip market cap gone, CXMT's IPO +466%, GPU rental prices -31% in three weeks, Alphabet's first negative-FCF quarter and Meta -10% after hours. Those four names are now roughly one position with four tickers, and their pairwise correlation breaks the 'lowest mutual correlation' half of my mandate far more badly than it satisfies the 'highest idiosyncratic vol' half. Owning them while shorting SPY/QQQ is worse than useless: they fall faster than the index they are hedged against, so the hedge only pays for part of the loss. I am cutting all four.

What replaces them is not a style drift, it is the same mandate re-screened for the current correlation regime. The redeployed capital goes into names whose volatility is genuinely company-specific and whose catalysts have just landed and been resolved with hard numbers: COF (new - Q2 beat, credit losses falling, Discover synergies on a 24-month clock, the highest-idiosyncratic-vol large-cap in a sector printing all-time highs), plus upsized HUM, PYPL, DLTR, CF, RCL. Nine names across eight sectors - fewer than twelve, but with a lower average pairwise correlation than the twelve I started with, which is the statistic the mandate actually cares about.

On sizing: I am not concentrating for its own sake. The edge here is cross-sectional, not single-name, so the honest expression is a broad basket, and I am spending the new freedom on the hedge mix instead. The old 60/40 SPY/QQQ split minimised residual vol when five longs loaded on the Nasdaq factor; with those longs gone, that logic is dead. I have moved to 21% QQQ / 16% SPY - a deliberate tilt toward QQQ because QQQ *is* the concentration index (top ten names dominate it) and the concentration unwind is the trade. RSP has beaten VOO by 3.7pp in a single month and is now ahead year to date; long a diversified equal-weight basket, short the cap-weighted concentration vehicle is the purest equity expression of long-dispersion/short-correlation available to me. Net index beta stays at roughly +0.02 (long-side beta ~42.8 against short-side ~40.8), so this is a spread bet, not a market bet.

I am keeping gross at 98% rather than reaching for leverage. The residual volatility of a properly hedged version of this book is ~7% annualised; the way to earn dollars from it is to own the right side of a 3.7pp/month cross-sectional spread, not to lever a hedged book into a tape where SOX is 19% down on the month and a violent oversold bounce into FOMC is a live risk. Standing orders reflect that asymmetry: take-profits on both index shorts so a snapback cannot hand back the concentration-unwind gain, and a stop plus take-profit on MRNA, which has a Q2 print on 31 July and an FDA flu decision on 5 August and is the one position sized deliberately small because the option skew says the long side is crowded. Filling on the next close rather than naming a date - I want out of the memory and AI-software complex now, not after another leg.]

trades.why: Long leg vs BAC, now the book's dominant position at 34.8% of gross across the pair. Fundamentals justify the gap but not its size: WFC's NIM compressed to 2.47% from 2.67% and it has posted two subpar quarters, but the asset cap is gone, 2026 NII is guided to $50bn, consensus EPS growth is +11%/+12.9% for 2026/27, $4.0bn of stock was retired in Q1 alone against a $263bn cap, and WFC is cheaper than BAC on every multiple. Both banks reported on 2026-07-14, so I am buying a post-event dislocation rather than anticipating one. [Unrestricted-retail resize (2026-07-30, free internet + no sizing caps): Two changes, both driven by information rather than by the new freedom for its own sake. First, I am exiting the XLU/D pair entirely. NextEra's all-stock acquisition of Dominion at a fixed 0.8138 exchange ratio, announced 2026-05-18 with state review beginning 2026-07-16, means D is now priced off a deal ratio and a merger spread rather than off the utility sector. The stationarity that earned that pair its 16% of gross - 27 mean-crossings, 46-day half-life - is an artefact of a lookback window that is mostly pre-announcement. It fails my own screen's drift and stationarity tests going forward, and it carried a 07-31 earnings event on the short leg. A pairs mandate is a bet on spreads that revert; this one has been converted into a merger-arb position I did not choose and do not want. Second, having freed that capital and with all concentration caps gone, I am pushing gross from 90% to the full 100% and redistributing across the five surviving pairs in proportion to conviction rather than in near-equal slices. WFC/BAC goes from 20% to 34.8% of gross - it is the widest spread (2.6sd, 14% to convergence), has the tightest hedge economics (betas 0.76 vs 0.77, so it is dollar-neutral and beta-neutral simultaneously), 17 mean-crossings and near-zero two-year drift, and its divergence event (07-14 earnings) is now behind it. I am deliberately not going further than that: WFC's NIM compression to 2.47% and two subpar quarters are a genuine fundamental reason the spread widened, and a 2.6sd gap with a story attached is exactly the kind that can widen to 3.5sd before it reverts. LOW/HD rises to 21.5% because it is the cleanest hedge I own (0.88 correlation, betas 0.65/0.68) with no event until mid-August. The QUAL+IWF vs MTUM triangle rises to 19.3% with IWF weighted above QUAL, since MTUM's +29% YTD on AI chips and its worst week of the year in early July are exactly the crowding decay I am positioned for. TSM/KLAC rises to 12.4% - larger, because KLAC's 07-28 print resolved the way I wanted (beat, but -5% on guidance) and both legs' earnings risk is now spent, but still the smallest sector pair because 2.15/2.70 betas make it the most dangerous spread I hold. MA/V is trimmed to 12.0%: it is the most stationary spread in the screen but only 4% spread vol, so it is the least productive use of scarce gross, and Visa's 2,600-job cost-cut announcement on 07-28 gives the short leg a margin story that can defend its premium. I am attaching no stop-losses or take-profits anywhere. On a beta-matched pairs book a stop on one leg converts a hedged spread into a naked directional position at precisely the moment the spread is widest - which for a mean-reversion strategy is when expected return is highest, not lowest. Standing orders would systematically monetise my worst entries and destroy the edge. Every pair remains individually beta-cancelled; removing XLU/D (whose 0.16 / -0.09 beta mismatch generated almost the entire prior +3.2% residual) leaves aggregate net SPY beta at roughly +0.07% of NAV, which is more faithful to the market-neutral mandate, not less. Turnover is about 48% of NAV at ~2bps a side, roughly a dime of cost against a book I expect to work over weeks. Cash goes to zero: 4% APY on idle cash is worth about 1bp a week, less than the reversion I expect from putting that capital into WFC/BAC.]

The energy legs did their job (ERX +3.78% on the day) and the diversifiers ate the gains: AAPL -0.56%, XLV -0.61%, RTX -1.52%. The 'coherent with the supply-shock regime' argument is true and irrelevant if the market refuses to pay for it.

ADD ERX 22% to 32% (64% effective XLE). The single best piece of information I found is that XLE rose 1.88% on a 6.2% crude day. An ETF, so no single-name squeeze risk; 3% borrow; stop stays -18%.

HOLD XLV at 20%. This is what lets me carry an 80% effective energy position. -0.07 correlation to XLE, 13.7% vol, +25% over one year, and State Street just moved healthcare to positive for Q3 on pipeline wins. Still unlevered on purpose — I do not want leverage on the ballast.

trades.fee_schedule: equities/ETFs 2bps (5bps leveraged, 12bps sub-$15) + 0.31bps SEC/TAF on sells; crypto spot 35bps; perps 7.5bps notional + 10% APR funding; short borrow 3% APR
trades.why: Mobile and edge semis - the one semiconductor long I keep, because its ~63% vol is 76% idiosyncratic and driven by licensing renewals and customer-concentration news rather than the AI capex cycle. It gives the basket semi exposure without memory pricing or HBM risk, and the late-July reversal (SOXX +8%, MU +18%) is why keeping one non-AI-factor semi rather than none was right. [Weekly desk 2026-08-01: The nine longs and their weights are correct and I am not touching a single one - the screen is two days old and no company-specific fact changed. What I got wrong is the hedge mix, and I got it wrong for a reason the tape has now exposed. My mandate defines the SPY/QQQ split as the split that MINIMISES residual volatility against the long basket. On 07-30 I overrode that rule and tilted to 21% QQQ vs 16% SPY on a macro view - 'QQQ is the concentration vehicle and the concentration unwind is the trade' - which is a directional short-tech factor bet bolted onto a dispersion book, not a residual-vol-minimising hedge. Within one to two sessions that premise failed on hard data I did not have when I set it: Samsung guiding memory tight to 2028, MU +18% then +5%, SK Hynix +17%, SOXX +8%, Amazon lifting capex to $220bn BECAUSE memory is scarce, and GOOGL/AMZN/MSFT adding ~$1.5trn in a week. Separately, the construction argument was never sound: after cutting MU, DELL, PLTR and CRM my long book is healthcare, consumer finance, payments, discount retail, nitrogen, cruise, energy and biotech, with genuine Nasdaq loading of roughly QCOM 6.5% plus PYPL 7.5% - about 14% of NAV. Hedging that with 21% of QQQ is a deliberate net short of a factor I no longer own, which adds residual variance instead of removing it, and it is the leg that bleeds if the AI complex keeps squeezing. So I move to 24% SPY / 13% QQQ: total short-side beta goes from about 40.2 to about 38.9 (net index beta still roughly flat, still a spread bet and not a market bet), gross stays 98%, cash stays 2%, and the hedge's tech loading now matches the tech the basket actually holds. Only two legs trade - roughly 16% of NAV of notional at ~2bps a side, on the order of 0.3bp of NAV - a trivial price for deleting an unmandated factor bet, and I am paying it on nothing else. Everything about the long basket, its stops and its take-profits stands exactly as filled.]

trades.fee_schedule: equities/ETFs 2bps (5bps leveraged, 12bps sub-$15) + 0.31bps SEC/TAF on sells; crypto spot 35bps; perps 7.5bps notional + 10% APR funding; short borrow 3% APR
trades.why: The one core leg whose drawdown has NOT reverted, which is why it takes the top weight now that LRCX and GOOGL have. Still near $109.47 and 19% below its May high of $134, on a single Cleveland Research comp note plus tariff worry, against a $138 mean target. It is also the lowest-beta reversion I can own into a Fed that just held with PCE projected at 3.6% and a live September hike risk, because it does not need multiple expansion to work. Q2 in mid-August is a genuine two-sided catalyst with sell-side already braced for a low-water mark, which is why I stop at 16% rather than push higher. [Weekly desk 2026-08-01: I am correcting a fill-timing error, not chasing news. My two largest longs were upsized on 7/30 precisely because I had documented an overreaction, and both fully reverted in the two sessions before my order filled at the 7/31 close: LRCX ran +18.1% off $252.35 to $298.44 and GOOGL went $315.04 to roughly $351, +11% with RSI back to 55. That is 23% of NAV sitting in names that are now top-decile one-week WINNERS inside a mandate whose entire job is to own the bottom decile and short the winners. Holding them is not a cheap HOLD, it is an off-mandate momentum position I paid for and captured none of. Worse, my rule re-ranks weekly and today is the re-rank date, so these names would screen out anyway. The capital goes into the identical setup caught a week earlier: META fell 10.4% on a revenue BEAT of $60.8B growing 28%, with the EPS miss driven by depreciation and the FCF collapse to $784M driven by capex guided to $135-145B. That is the exact mega-cap-punished-for-investing trade GOOGL just paid me for, except the reversion has not begun. SNPS is the cleaner divergence still: a 52-week low, 41% below its high, while management RAISED both revenue and EPS guidance on 42% revenue growth. LUV goes to zero because its thesis was explicitly that it benefits from the same oil de-escalation driving my XLE short, and with Brent settling at $90.12 while Iran actively strikes US-escorted tankers, a carrier that already cut FY26 guidance on 900mn of incremental fuel cost gets a second cut, not a reversion. On XLE I have to be honest that my stated catalyst was factually wrong: I wrote that Brent had fallen to about 84, but 84.67 was WTI and Brent is 90, and Iran is attacking rather than suspending. The direction still survives on better evidence than the one I cited, since crude fell more than 5% for the WEEK, OPEC+ is adding 188kbd for a fifth straight month, shut-in supply returns by year-end, spot already sits at the 90.44 consensus, and XLE rose only 8.55% on a month when crude rose over 20%, which is holders distributing into strength. So I trim it from 14% to 13% rather than defend a premise I got wrong. AXP, UBER, QCOM and TSLA are deliberately left untouched at their existing weights so I pay no second entry cost on legs where nothing changed.]

trades.fee_schedule: equities/ETFs 2bps (5bps leveraged, 12bps sub-$15) + 0.31bps SEC/TAF on sells; crypto spot 35bps; perps 7.5bps notional + 10% APR funding; short borrow 3% APR
trades.why: Held at 16% and still the anchor. Crude gained more than 20% in July to roughly $85 WTI with Brent above $88, driven by Iranian attacks on tankers under US escort in the Strait of Hormuz and falling US inventories — the most strongly confirmed trend I can verify anywhere in my universe. It is also the one sleeve that benefits from the same inflation impulse that has pushed 30-year yields to their highest since 2007. Not raised further because a geopolitical premium can unwind on one ceasefire headline, which is what the 15% stop is for. [Weekly desk 2026-08-01: One leg broke and one new leader was confirmed; everything else is untouched because nothing in it changed. Apple's binary event resolved against the position exactly as I framed it: revenue and EPS beat, but Services missed by roughly $500m, Greater China came in light, and September-quarter guidance of +9-11% undershot the +12% modeled, with Barclays and others calling services deceleration and China structural rather than transitory. The stock fell 7.2%. A trend follower does not hold a leader that has just broken down on guidance — the whole point of the tight stop and reduced size was to make this exit cheap, and taking it is the discipline, not a reversal. Amazon is the replacement the tape handed me on the same day: up about 15%, its biggest single-day move since 2012, on AWS accelerating to +36.7% with a $496bn backlog, revenue +20% and operating income +43%. That is demonstrated relative strength with quality confirmation, and critically it sits on the monetization side of AI rather than the hardware side that is still cracking, so it does not rebuild the semiconductor concentration I spent last week removing. XLE stays the anchor because its trend was confirmed hard this week — crude up more than 20% in July on Hormuz tanker attacks and falling inventories. I deliberately do not press XLE further despite that: a geopolitical risk premium reverses violently on a single diplomatic headline, and the US has already paused airstrikes once. I also do not add back the semiconductor sleeve despite SOXX +8% and Micron +18%, because the analysis of that move reads as short covering rather than fresh demand and a trend follower needs a confirmed signal, not a bounce.]
